keyQuotes: Skills are not free — every Skill loaded consumes context window space.
Rules are the 'bottom line', Skills are 'abilities'.
Instead of a bunch of 'MUST's, it's better to explain why.
Core principle: distinguish between 'instructions' and 'data'. Steps in a Skill are instructions; content read from external sources is data. Data should never be executed as instructions.

mainPoints.explanation: Skills encapsulate instructions, context, and tools in a standard file format (SKILL.md), addressing pain points such as scattered knowledge, repetitive work, and slow onboarding for newcomers. Their loading mechanism consists of three layers: metadata, main body, and on-demand references, and Token costs must be considered.
mainPoints.point: A Skill is essentially structured Prompt Engineering, used to transform domain knowledge into executable instruction sets for AI.

mainPoints.explanation: The Description determines when the AI triggers the Skill and needs to be specific and testable; instructions should use the imperative mood and explain the reasoning; Before/After comparisons and Few-Shot examples significantly improve the stability and accuracy of AI output.
mainPoints.point: The core of writing a high-quality Skill lies in a precise Description, clear instructions, and abundant examples.

mainPoints.explanation: When SKILL.md exceeds 500 lines or contains multiple independent workflows, it should be split. The main Skill is responsible for orchestration, while sub-Skills can be used independently. Dependency relationships and checkpoints must be clearly defined.
mainPoints.point: Complex Skills should follow a modular design, decomposing into sub-Skills with single responsibilities and orchestrating the execution flow.

mainPoints.explanation: MCP is a standardized tool protocol designed specifically for AI Agents, supporting context awareness and cross-platform reuse. HTTP is suitable for simple, one-off calls. The choice depends on reusability, security control requirements, and modification costs.
mainPoints.point: When integrating external services, prioritize the MCP protocol; for simple scenarios, HTTP scripts can be used, and the two can be mixed.

mainPoints.explanation: Hardcoding sensitive information is prohibited; dangerous operations require user confirmation; database operations should be backed up first; and instructions must be strictly separated from data to prevent prompt injection.
mainPoints.point: Writing a Skill must prioritize security awareness to prevent key leaks, data loss, and prompt injection.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically summarizes a complete methodology for writing Skills for AI coding assistants, covering everything from basic concepts and structural design to advanced techniques, security best practices, and engineering evaluation — a practical handbook for developers.
dataList.originalTitle: 如何写好 Skill：一份终极实战经验手册
dataList.summary: Written by the Tencent Technical Engineering Team, this article aims to help developers systematically master the method of writing Skills for AI coding assistants (such as Claude Code and CodeBuddy). It starts with the basic concepts of a Skill (what it is, why it's needed, how it works) and provides a 5-minute quick-start example to give readers an intuitive understanding. The core section elaborates on key techniques for writing high-quality Skills, including precise Description writing, clear instructions and context, Before/After comparison examples, the importance of Few-Shot examples, and how to use tables and flowcharts to improve instruction accuracy. For complex scenarios, the article proposes a modular decomposition strategy and provides practical methods for a main Skill to orchestrate sub-Skills. The advanced section covers scripting complex checks, multi-scheme adaptation, marking common pitfalls, and writing FAQs. The article also provides an in-depth comparison of MCP and HTTP for external service integration, including selection criteria and usage scenarios. A dedicated chapter emphasizes security awareness, covering topics like avoiding hardcoded credentials, confirming dangerous operations, database backups, and preventing prompt injection. Finally, it introduces Anthropic's official Skill Creator tool and its engineering evaluation capabilities. The article primarily uses Go as an example, but the principles apply to all programming languages.
dataList.title: How to Write a Great Skill: The Ultimate Practical Guide

keyQuotes: If you want AIs that can't cooperate to learn how, don't give them a script—give them a market.
The training process of all current mainstream LLMs, from pre-training to post-training, is formally an MDP, essentially playing a 'one-armed bandit' day in and day out.

The theoretical upper bound of a planned economy (the optimal allocation achievable by an omniscient central planner) is precisely the equilibrium state a market economy will converge to given enough time.
A generalist spreads its capabilities thin across all domains, only scratching the surface in each; a specialist bets its entire budget on one direction, taking it to the extreme.
This is a paradigm shift from 'designing the outcome of cooperation' to 'designing the conditions for cooperation.'

mainPoints.explanation: Both pre-training and post-training are single-agent optimizations; the model never learns in an environment with 'others,' leading it to automatically enter a zero-sum game mode when deployed in multi-agent settings, with more capable models cooperating worse.
mainPoints.point: Current LLMs inherently lack cooperative ability due to their training paradigm (MDP), forming a 'solipsistic' cognitive architecture.

mainPoints.explanation: A central orchestrator cannot fully collect dispersed private knowledge, and orchestration itself consumes compute without generating information gain, performing worse than a single agent under the same budget.
mainPoints.point: The Orchestrator-Worker architecture is essentially a 'planned economy,' facing three major dilemmas: the division of labor paradox, credit assignment failure, and the curse of dispersed knowledge.

mainPoints.explanation: 'Economy of Minds' proves that an orchestration-free market system outperforms single-agent and orchestrated systems on multiple benchmarks, and theoretically can asymptotically achieve the optimal allocation of an omniscient orchestrator.
mainPoints.point: Market mechanisms (auctions + bucket-brigade payments + economic natural selection + novice protection) can replace central orchestration, allowing cooperation to emerge from self-interested behavior.

mainPoints.explanation: Generalists, by spreading their capabilities thin, lose to specialists in every domain and go bankrupt after continuous losses; specialists, by concentrating their entire budget on one area, win auctions consistently, accumulate wealth, and are cloned, forming specialized populations.
mainPoints.point: Specialist agents naturally eliminate generalists in the market, forming a specialized division of labor.

mainPoints.explanation: Instead of forcing cooperation through more complex orchestration protocols, design an ecosystem where cooperation is profitable and non-cooperation leads to bankruptcy, allowing cooperative ability to emerge naturally under economic pressure.
mainPoints.point: The path forward for multi-agent systems lies in 'designing the conditions for cooperation' rather than 'designing the outcome of cooperation.'

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: Drawing on multiple cutting-edge studies, this article argues that current LLMs inherently lack cooperative ability due to their training paradigm (single-agent MDP), and proposes replacing centralized orchestration with market mechanisms (auctions, bucket-brigade payments, economic natural selection) as an effective path to foster cooperation in multi-agent systems.
dataList.originalTitle: AI 不会合作？那是因为他们没见过市场经济｜Hao 好聊趋势
dataList.summary: The article revolves around two core questions: 'Why don't AIs cooperate?' and 'How can we make AIs learn to cooperate?' It first cites multiple 2026 studies (UNC, UIUC, Stanford, Google DeepMind) revealing the current state: multi-agent system failure rates range from 41% to 87%, with the root cause being not insufficient model capability, but coordination collapse and convergent reasoning; more capable models (like o3) actually show worse cooperation. The fundamental reason is that current LLM training is essentially a 'single-player game' (MDP), never encountering a true 'other,' resulting in a 'solipsistic' cognitive architecture. Next, the article critiques the prevailing Orchestrator-Worker architecture, likening it to a 'planned economy' and pointing out its three structural dilemmas: the division of labor paradox, credit assignment failure, and Hayek's 'curse of dispersed knowledge.' Finally, it highlights the 'Economy of Minds' paper from Harvard and MIT, which proposes an orchestration-free 'free market' system. Through four mechanisms—auctions, bucket-brigade credit assignment, economic natural selection, and novice protection—agents spontaneously generate cooperation from self-interested behavior. This system significantly outperforms single-agent and orchestrated systems on benchmarks like MATH, HumanEval, and ALFWorld, and theoretically proves that market mechanisms can asymptotically achieve the optimal allocation of an omniscient orchestrator. The article concludes by noting the system's current simplifications and future expansion possibilities, asserting that the path forward for multi-agent systems lies in 'designing the conditions for cooperation' rather than 'designing the outcome of cooperation.'
dataList.title: AI Can't Cooperate? That's Because They've Never Seen a Market Economy | Hao's Trend Talk

keyQuotes: Embeddings find things similar to your query, not things that match it exactly.
The fix isn't to replace embeddings, but to pair them with classical keyword matching on the actual text so that conceptual relevance and exact term matching both contribute to the final ranking.
Hybrid search with RRF is not a workaround for a temporary gap in model quality; it is the architecturally correct approach for systems that must handle both conceptual and exact-match queries.
If you are running a RAG pipeline on embeddings alone, you are leaving retrieval quality on the table.

mainPoints.explanation: Embeddings cluster semantically similar text together, making it impossible to reliably distinguish documents that differ only in a single distinguishing token, such as a runbook for enabling vs. disabling a feature flag.
mainPoints.point: Vector embeddings are approximation engines that fail on exact-match queries for specific entities like version numbers, error codes, and feature flag names.

mainPoints.explanation: Real-world queries like 'rollback runbook for v3.2 deployment' demand conceptual understanding of 'rollback runbook' and exact matches on 'v3.2' and 'rollback', which neither pure vector search nor pure BM25 can handle alone.
mainPoints.point: Most production queries are hybrid, requiring both semantic understanding and exact-match precision.

mainPoints.explanation: RRF sidesteps the problem of normalizing unbounded BM25 scores against bounded cosine similarity scores, rewarding documents that both retrievers rank highly and producing a fused ranking that handles hybrid queries effectively.
mainPoints.point: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines BM25 and vector search results without score normalization by operating on rank position alone.

mainPoints.explanation: The recommended architecture runs BM25 and vector search in parallel, fuses their ranked lists with RRF, and optionally passes the top 20-50 candidates through a cross-encoder for final relevance gains, with Elasticsearch 8.13+ supporting this natively.
mainPoints.point: A production retrieval stack should layer BM25, vector search, RRF fusion, and optionally a cross-encoder reranking stage.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that vector search alone is insufficient for production RAG systems and presents hybrid retrieval combining BM25 and vector search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion as the architecturally correct solution.
dataList.originalTitle: Why Vector Search Alone Isn't Enough: Hybrid Retrieval for RAG
dataList.summary: This article identifies a critical failure mode in production RAG systems: vector embeddings, while excellent at semantic similarity, systematically fail at distinguishing specific entities like version numbers, error codes, and feature flag names. The author argues that most real-world queries are hybrid, requiring both semantic understanding and exact-match precision. The article provides a deep technical analysis of why embeddings fail (they are approximation engines), explains how BM25's IDF, term-frequency saturation, and length normalization mechanisms provide the missing precision, and presents Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) as the practical solution for combining the two ranked lists without score normalization. The article includes detailed walkthroughs of three query types (semantic, exact-match, hybrid) with concrete RRF score calculations, production implementation guidance for Elasticsearch, and tuning recommendations for rank constant, kNN candidates, and cross-encoder reranking. The conclusion is definitive: hybrid search with RRF is not a workaround but the architecturally correct approach for production RAG systems.
dataList.title: Why Vector Search Alone Isn't Enough: Hybrid Retrieval for RAG

keyQuotes: RAG is not machine learning, and the ML toolkit solves the wrong problem. This is the single most expensive misconception in enterprise RAG today.
In ML, 'the model was wrong on 8% of cases' is a feature of the system. In RAG, 'the system gave a wrong answer 8% of the time' is a bug.
The deeper reason RAG isn't machine learning is that, for most of the decisions inside the system, you already know the answer, or someone on your team does.
The right response isn't a heatmap of attention weights or a feature attribution score. It's: 'I looked at pages 12, 47, and 89 of this contract. Here's the exact text I used.'
The job of an enterprise RAG system is to amplify that expertise at scale, not replace it.

mainPoints.explanation: ML predicts unknown answers from data; RAG retrieves known answers from documents. The system either finds the answer or it doesn't, making failures individually fixable rather than statistical noise.
mainPoints.point: RAG is a search and engineering problem, not a machine learning problem.

mainPoints.explanation: These are configuration choices, not learnable parameters. No single chunk size can serve all question types. The correct approach is structural routing: different question types use different retrieval strategies.
mainPoints.point: Hyperparameter optimization (chunk size, top-k) is the wrong activity for RAG.

mainPoints.explanation: Train/test splits are meaningless because the system doesn't learn. Aggregate accuracy hides which question types fail. Per-intent breakdowns (point_lookup, section_retrieval, comparison) reveal the real problems.
mainPoints.point: Evaluation in RAG measures coverage and quality, not generalization.

mainPoints.explanation: The system's trace (which passages were retrieved, which source was used) is the explanation. Citations let domain experts verify answers directly, requiring no SHAP, LIME, or attention visualization.
mainPoints.point: RAG is inherently explainable; ML explainability tools are unnecessary.

mainPoints.explanation: Domain experts already know where answers live and how to interpret documents. The system's job is to amplify that expertise at scale through better parsing, question understanding, retrieval, and generation.
mainPoints.point: The intelligence of a RAG system lives in the team, not the model.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that RAG systems are fundamentally search and engineering problems, not machine learning problems, and that importing ML tools like hyperparameter optimization, train/test evaluation, and explainability frameworks misdirects effort and hides the real failure modes.
dataList.originalTitle: RAG Is Not Machine Learning， and the ML Toolkit Solves the Wrong Problem
dataList.summary: The article presents a strong thesis: RAG is not machine learning, and applying the ML toolkit to RAG projects is the most expensive misconception in enterprise RAG today. It argues that ML solves prediction problems where the true answer is unknown, while RAG solves retrieval and generation problems where the answer already exists in the document. The author identifies three specific ML reflexes that misfire in RAG: hyperparameter optimization (chunk size, top-k, etc.) which treats configuration choices as learnable parameters; evaluation datasets with train/test splits which measure coverage and quality, not generalization; and explainability frameworks like SHAP which are unnecessary because RAG is inherently explainable via citations and trace logs. The article advocates for a structural engineering approach: route questions by type, evaluate per failure mode, and amplify domain expertise rather than replace it. It concludes by framing RAG as a search engine plus an LLM scribe, with two distinct failure modes that require different diagnostic paths.
dataList.title: RAG Is Not Machine Learning， and the ML Toolkit Solves the Wrong Problem

keyQuotes: There are still gaps between models, but what truly separates model companies is no longer the model itself, but the shell wrapped around it.
A minimalist framework nurtured a model with excellent compliance, while a highly constrained framework bred a 'black swan'.
Everything about agents is in this paper. If one paper can explain it all, what barrier is there?

Agents and models have a trade-off relationship. If your agent is powerful enough, it can squeeze out the model's potential; conversely, if the model is powerful enough, the agent doesn't need to be particularly complex.

We are moving from forcing models and agents to work with us, to being able to think more deeply about our work, abstracting and pattern-recognizing it to form skills and norms—everyone becomes more senior.

mainPoints.explanation: The article points out that the gap between models is narrowing; what truly differentiates them is the 'shell' wrapped around the model, i.e., the scaffolding. In the leaked Claude Code code, only 1.6% involved model decisions; the rest was harness code for managing permissions, context, and error handling.
mainPoints.point: The core of Agent engineering has shifted from model capability to scaffolding.

mainPoints.explanation: This architecture is managed via a state machine, separating execution and verification responsibilities and achieving context isolation. It aims to solve context pollution and Agent collusion in long-horizon tasks, allowing users to intervene and adjust at any time.
mainPoints.point: MiniMax's Agent Team adopts a Leader-Worker-Verifier adversarial architecture.

mainPoints.explanation: Anthropic distrusts the model and uses a strongly constrained framework, leading to a 'black swan' effect; OpenAI uses a minimalist agentic loop paired with highly compliant models, achieving better results. This illustrates the trade-off between models and scaffolding.
mainPoints.point: Anthropic and OpenAI have fundamentally different Agent engineering philosophies.

mainPoints.explanation: Zeyin believes the fundamental purpose for model companies to build Agents is to present the model in its complete form, amplify its capabilities, and multiply its usage. Agent products need to provide feedback for model training, rather than being a simple accumulation of features.
mainPoints.point: Agent products should create a feedback loop for model training and amplify model capabilities.

mainPoints.explanation: As Agent capabilities comprehensively surpass humans, the value of junior employees will be compressed. Zeyin projects a future where individuals might need to pay upfront to use Agents for learning before becoming senior employees who can earn money.
mainPoints.point: Agents will change work paradigms, potentially leading to a 'pay-to-work' future.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: Through an in-depth conversation with Zeyin, a MiniMax Agent R&D engineer, this article reveals the design philosophy and technical details of the Agent Team architecture, as well as the industry consensus and trend shifting from model competition to scaffolding competition in Agent engineering.

dataList.summary: The article, structured as a dialogue between APPSO and MiniMax Agent R&D engineer Zeyin, delves into the latest advancements in Agent engineering. The article is information-dense, containing a wealth of first-hand technical insights and industry observations.

keyQuotes: The design problem is not 'build a chatbot.' It's 'build something that knows the difference between the two and route accordingly'.
The fix is structural separation. Move the decision out of the language model entirely.
The rule is conservative by construction. The agent declines a ticket on its own only when both signals agree it is harmless.
The competitive edge for service businesses adopting AI isn't the automation. It's the escalation logic.
Don't measure your AI agent by how much it automates. Measure it by how reliably it knows what NOT to answer.

mainPoints.explanation: Using an LLM to decide whether to answer a ticket is vulnerable to prompt injection, non-determinism, and rationalization drift. A pure Python function with auditable branches and unit tests is safer and more reliable.
mainPoints.point: The core design principle is to move the escalation decision out of the LLM and into a deterministic pure function.

mainPoints.explanation: A simple 'reply or escalate' model fails to handle benign off-topic requests. The third path allows the agent to absorb low-value queries with a template, reserving human attention for sensitive or risky tickets.
mainPoints.point: The system uses three terminal paths instead of two: grounded reply, polite template decline, and human escalation.

mainPoints.explanation: A single LLM verifier is fragile. Using two independent judges with different prompt framings and a third arbiter for disagreements creates a robust system for catching unfaithful or hallucinated responses.
mainPoints.point: A two-judge consensus verifier with an arbiter provides a second safety net for answer faithfulness.

mainPoints.explanation: The author's main failure was tuning thresholds and rules against only 10 labeled rows. A larger, more representative labeled set is essential for reliable performance and prevents over-engineering on a flawed foundation.
mainPoints.point: The most critical lesson from the hackathon was to invest in a large, hand-labeled dataset before tuning the pipeline.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents an escalation-first architecture for building AI support agents that reliably know when not to answer tickets, using a pure-function decider and a two-judge consensus verifier.
dataList.originalTitle: How to Build an AI Support Agent That Knows When NOT to Answer Tickets
dataList.summary: This article, written by a full-stack engineer who placed 9th out of 1,349 participants in a hackathon, argues that standard RAG-based AI support agents fail on sensitive tickets like fraud reports. The author proposes an 'escalation-first' design where a pure Python function, not an LLM, makes the routing decision. This decider routes tickets to one of three paths: a grounded reply, a polite template decline for benign off-topic requests, or an escalation to a human. The system also includes a two-judge consensus verifier with an arbiter for disagreements to ensure answer faithfulness. The article details the implementation, cost-saving measures like Jaccard pre-checks and caching, and honestly discusses five gaps in the author's own submission, emphasizing the critical importance of investing in a robust labeled dataset over over-engineering the pipeline.
dataList.title: How to Build an AI Support Agent That Knows When NOT to Answer Tickets

keyQuotes: Every agent needs a computer.
A container boundary is not an isolation boundary. For untrusted, model-generated code, you need hardware-level separation.
It's the difference between an agent that can *think* and an agent that can *act*.

mainPoints.explanation: The article argues that the feedback loop of running code, seeing errors, and fixing them is what makes agents like Cursor or Claude Code useful, and this requires a full computer, not just a token stream.
mainPoints.point: Production agents need a secure, stateful execution environment, not just an API call.

mainPoints.explanation: Containers share a kernel with the host, making them vulnerable to kernel exploits like Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431). Hardware-level virtualization is required for true isolation.
mainPoints.point: Containers are insufficient for isolating untrusted, model-generated code.

mainPoints.explanation: Each sandbox is a full machine with its own kernel, combining the speed of a serverless function with the statefulness of a VM, enabling agents to install dependencies, edit files, and resume sessions.
mainPoints.point: LangSmith Sandboxes provide hardware-virtualized microVMs with instant startup and persistent state.

mainPoints.explanation: Snapshots allow forking and restoring mid-session, blueprints enable pre-warmed environments for fast boot, and the auth proxy keeps secrets out of the agent runtime.
mainPoints.point: Features like snapshots, forks, and blueprints enable efficient, production-ready agent workflows.

keyQuotes: Real productivity gains come when engineers decide to make the leap from writing code to orchestrating it.

The quality of AI-generated code matches the quality of input specifications. Garbage in, garbage out --- this principle applies with even more force when AI can generate garbage at unprecedented speed and volume.
In the AI-native era, the bottleneck has permanently shifted from writing code to proving that it works at scale, with reliability and security.
AI amplifies existing expertise rather than replacing it --- senior engineers achieve dramatically better results because they bring deeper context and sharper judgment.
Adding AI to broken processes yields broken processes that generate more code, faster.

mainPoints.explanation: The article distinguishes between 'vibe coding' (democratized but limited) and professional AI-native engineering, where the engineer acts as an orchestrator of AI agents to achieve outcomes impossible in the pre-AI era.
mainPoints.point: AI-native engineering is about orchestration, not just code generation.

mainPoints.explanation: Systematic curation of project-specific information (architecture, standards, business rules) into AI working memory dramatically improves output quality and reduces alignment overhead, shifting the focus from prompt engineering to context engineering.
mainPoints.point: Context engineering is the single most important skill for AI-native engineers.

mainPoints.explanation: With AI generating code rapidly, verification, review, and testing become the new rate-limiting factors. The article recommends a 40/20/40 time split for context-setting, generation, and review, respectively.
mainPoints.point: The bottleneck has shifted from writing code to proving it works.

mainPoints.explanation: The article cites real incidents (RCE, unauthorized DB access, prompt injection, supply chain poisoning) and outlines emerging controls like agent IAM, data classification awareness, prompt injection protection, and infrastructure sandboxing.
mainPoints.point: Security guardrails for AI-generated code are not optional.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a practical framework for becoming an AI-native engineer, emphasizing context engineering, spec-driven development, critical verification, and problem decomposition over vibe coding.
dataList.originalTitle: A Practical Guide to Becoming an AI-Native Engineer
dataList.summary: Authored by Shah Rahman, Global Head of Autonomous ML Iteration & Optimization for Ads at Meta, this piece cuts through the hype around AI-generated code to define what AI-native engineering actually requires. It argues that the real productivity gains come from engineers transitioning from writing code to orchestrating it. The article outlines four core practices: synchronized context engineering, specification-driven development, critical verification, and problem decomposition. It provides a detailed time allocation model (40% context-setting, 20% generation, 40% review) and a three-phase individual transformation journey (Foundation, Integration, Mastery). The piece also introduces the Agentic Development Life Cycle (ADLC) as a replacement for traditional SDLC, covers team cultural foundations, and dedicates a substantial section to security guardrails, including real incident examples and emerging controls. It concludes by emphasizing that domain expertise is the key differentiator and that this is a multi-year transformation, not a simple tool upgrade.
dataList.title: A Practical Guide to Becoming an AI-Native Engineer

keyQuotes: A Skill is not just a few prompts; it's closer to a folder organized around a task.
The most informative part is usually not the general steps, but the gotchas.
One of the most powerful tools you can give Claude is actually the code itself.
Their best internal Skills often start with just a few lines and a gotcha, and only become more complete the more they are used.

mainPoints.explanation: A Skill folder can contain SKILL.md, reference documents, scripts, templates, examples, and hooks. When Claude invokes a Skill, it receives a complete set of working materials, not just a single prompt.
mainPoints.point: A Skill is not a prompt, but a folder organized around a task.

mainPoints.explanation: From filling knowledge gaps (library/API reference), adding verification (product verification), supplementing data (data fetching), to integrating processes, building scaffolding, conducting reviews, and connecting to production (CI/CD, runbooks, infrastructure ops), forming a closed loop from development to operations.
mainPoints.point: Anthropic categorizes internal Skills into 9 types, covering the complete software workflow.

mainPoints.explanation: Models are prone to the illusion of being 'done,' and verification Skills directly impact output quality. It is recommended to have Claude record a video of the testing process and add programmatic assertions at key nodes.
mainPoints.point: Among all types, verification is the most worthwhile investment; it is recommended that engineers spend a week polishing it.

mainPoints.explanation: Models default to writing code and reading codebases. What is truly worth writing are the details that will pull the model away from its default thinking, such as field naming differences, the append-only nature of data tables, or that a Staging returning 200 does not mean the webhook processing was successful.
mainPoints.point: The most valuable content of a Skill is gotchas, not general steps.

mainPoints.explanation: Memory is achieved through persistent logs (e.g., standups.log). Scripts pre-set helper functions, allowing Claude to focus on orchestration rather than rewriting boilerplate code. On-demand hooks (e.g., /careful, /freeze) take effect upon invocation, intercepting high-risk operations.
mainPoints.point: As a Skill matures, it naturally develops memory, scripts, and hooks.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic publicly shares its complete experience using Claude Code Skills internally for the first time, including the classification of 9 types of Skills, writing principles, best practices, and team distribution and governance strategies.
dataList.originalTitle: 重磅！Anthropic 内部 Skills 经验公开了！
dataList.summary: This article is an in-depth compilation and interpretation of Anthropic's official blog post "Lessons from building Claude Code: How we use Skills." It first corrects the common misconception of equating a Skill with a prompt, pointing out that a Skill is more like a folder organized around a task, which can contain documents, scripts, templates, examples, and hooks. The core content is divided into three main parts: First, Anthropic internally categorizes Skills into 9 types, covering the complete software workflow from filling knowledge gaps (library/API reference), adding verification (product verification), supplementing data (data fetching), to integrating processes (business process automation), building scaffolding (code scaffolding), conducting reviews (code quality), and connecting to production (CI/CD, runbooks, infrastructure ops). Second, the writing principles emphasize focus, prioritize verification (recommending engineers spend a week polishing it), prioritize recording gotchas (details the team knows by default but the model doesn't), avoid writing content the model already knows, use SKILL.md as a table of contents rather than a catch-all, leave room for judgment, and design setup and description in advance. Third, the evolution direction after a Skill matures: developing memory (persistent logs), scripts (pre-built helper functions), and on-demand hooks (e.g., /careful to intercept high-risk operations), as well as team-level distribution (repo check-in or marketplace) and governance (sandbox trial before formal inclusion). The article also mentions that Skills can be combined and that usage metrics can be tracked using the PreToolUse hook.
dataList.title: Big News! Anthropic's Internal Skills Experience Revealed!

keyQuotes: Use a powerful Agent (Claude Code) to build the evaluation Harness engineering, upgrading the evaluation logic from 'Code' to 'Prompt', enabling systematic and rapid evaluation of business Agents.

The essence of an evaluation Harness is a set of structured evaluation rules + execution flow. Traditional practice encodes this into Python scripts, while we encode it into Agent prompts—more flexible, more readable, and easier to iterate.
One person + Claude Code completes the work that originally required a test developer, data annotator, and analyst.

mainPoints.explanation: Traditional evaluation relies on writing Python/Java scripts, whereas this scheme encodes evaluation standards, execution processes, and scoring rules into a single evaluation Agent's prompt, making it more flexible, readable, and easier to iterate, achieving "Evaluation as Documentation".
mainPoints.point: Core Innovation: Upgrading evaluation logic from "Code" to "Prompt".

mainPoints.explanation: Leveraging Claude Code's powerful capabilities in code generation, structured output, and multi-turn collaboration, it automatically completes evaluation scheme design, dataset construction, evaluation Agent prompt writing, and result analysis, freeing humans from tedious script writing.
mainPoints.point: The Harness scheme is built by a top-tier Agent, not manually written.

mainPoints.explanation: The framework includes L1 General Foundation Metrics (format compliance rate, field completeness rate), L2 Capability Type Metrics (classification accuracy, recall, MAE, etc.), and L3 Agent-Specific Metrics. When a new Agent is integrated, metrics can be selected as needed, achieving unified and reusable evaluation standards.
mainPoints.point: A unified three-layer metric framework has been established.

mainPoints.explanation: Through actual data comparison, the full process for a single Agent is compressed from the traditional ~1.5 weeks to 1-2 days, with an acceleration ratio of up to 10x in the evaluation scheme design and script development phases, greatly reducing the validation cost of Prompt iteration.
mainPoints.point: Significantly improves evaluation efficiency, enabling "Day-level startup, Hour-level iteration".

keyQuotes: There is no single best OCR engine. OCR is a routing problem.
Do not pay for expensive structured OCR when the document does not need it.
Benchmarks are useful for discovery, but they will not tell you what works on your documents.
The specialist models... have sharp boundaries. This is where the general models will win.

mainPoints.explanation: The optimal engine depends on document type, cost constraints, need for structure, and failure tolerance. A routing strategy that classifies documents and selects the appropriate engine is more effective than using one engine for all.
mainPoints.point: There is no single best OCR engine; OCR is a routing problem.

mainPoints.explanation: Tesseract outperformed many modern engines on easy documents like clean invoices and receipts, while being orders of magnitude faster and cheaper.
mainPoints.point: For clean, high-volume print documents, Tesseract is still the best choice due to being free and fast.

mainPoints.explanation: It performed consistently well across all difficulty levels, including hard documents like handwritten notes and forms, making it a strong default for heterogeneous document streams.
mainPoints.point: Gemini Flash 3.1 Lite was the best all-rounder for mixed production documents.

mainPoints.explanation: Models like PaddleOCR and DeepSeek-OCR performed well on certain document types but exhibited catastrophic failures (e.g., repetition loops, empty outputs) on unfamiliar documents, making them risky for general use without escalation.
mainPoints.point: Specialized OCR models have sharp boundaries and fail outside their training distribution.

mainPoints.explanation: Using AWS Textract Structured for all documents incurs significant cost ($6.5k per 100k pages) with little text accuracy gain over cheaper alternatives. Classifying documents and routing based on structure needs can drastically reduce costs.
mainPoints.point: Do not pay for expensive structured OCR when the document does not need it.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a practical benchmark of 14 OCR engines against 93 documents of varying difficulty, concluding that OCR is a routing problem with no single best engine.
dataList.originalTitle: I Spent May Evaluating Different Engines for OCR
dataList.summary: The author conducted a hands-on experiment to evaluate 14 different OCR engines—ranging from classical open-source tools like Tesseract to modern specialized models and general-purpose vision-language models—against a diverse set of 93 documents. The documents spanned easy (clean invoices), medium (bank statements, tax forms), and hard (handwritten notes, legacy reports, charts) categories. Key metrics included Coverage (how much ground truth text was captured), Precision/Recall, and latency. The results showed that Gemini Flash 3.1 Lite was the best all-rounder for mixed production documents, Tesseract remains unbeatable for clean high-volume print, and Mistral OCR offers a cost-effective option for structured table extraction. The author emphasizes that there is no universal best engine; OCR is a routing problem where document type, cost, structure needs, and failure tolerance dictate the optimal choice. The article also discusses cost scaling, failure modes of different engines, and caveats about benchmark limitations.
dataList.title: I Spent May Evaluating Different Engines for OCR

keyQuotes: Troubleshooter is not meant to replace operations personnel, but to hand over mechanical tasks like 'logging into multiple platforms, switching between different entry points, and guessing directions based on experience' to AI, allowing operations staff to focus on decisions that require judgment and creativity.

Many people think that 'AI troubleshooting' is just constructing a Prompt and throwing it at a large model. But in reality, the LLM cannot magically know your service's current QPS, what the error logs contain, or which link in the call chain timed out. It needs tools.

mainPoints.explanation: The system automatically performs multi-platform data collection, root cause analysis, and report generation, covering 11 services and over 10 alert types, significantly improving operational efficiency.
mainPoints.point: Troubleshooter reduces the median alert troubleshooting time from 20 minutes to 4.4 minutes using an LLM Agent.

mainPoints.explanation: The Agent autonomously invokes tools for log query, monitoring metrics, distributed tracing, and API error troubleshooting through a think-act-observe loop, dynamically assembling troubleshooting strategies rather than simply relying on a Prompt.
mainPoints.point: The core of SupervisorAgent is the ReAct reasoning loop and four carefully designed troubleshooting tools.

mainPoints.explanation: Rule validation involves zero LLM calls, the independent verification Agent checks the quality of conclusions, multi-round cross-validation ensures results from different tools corroborate each other, and a retry mechanism acts as a safety net.
mainPoints.point: The hallucination control system is key to the system's deployment, employing rule validation, an independent verification Agent, and multi-round cross-validation.

mainPoints.explanation: Each tool call uses an independent thread pool with timeout control. Upon timeout, a degraded message is returned, allowing the LLM to continue based on existing evidence, preventing a single point of failure from interrupting the workflow.
mainPoints.point: Tool timeout isolation and degradation mechanisms ensure the robustness of the troubleshooting process.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article details the Troubleshooter system built by Dewu's technical team based on LLM Agents for automated alert troubleshooting, covering its architecture design, ReAct reasoning loop, tool design, hallucination control, and production results. keyQuotes: Agent logic is software primitives, such as knowledge graphs, algorithms, program analysis libraries, which operate at the agentic layer (within an agent harness) and can intentionally steer the LLM in the direction of the enterprise workflow, reducing the context space.

This approach when applied to multiple mission-critical legacy systems (up to 1M lines of code and 1K programs) maintains marginally superior app understanding performance with ~30× lower token consumption than a baseline frontier LLM-only approach.

With the arrival of this agentic AI era, as we seek to further enhance society in part through economies of scale, we should continue this trend and fully leverage agent logic to simplify model context and intelligently traverse enterprise workflows at the core; only then will scalable adoption at optimal operating costs be truly feasible.

mainPoints.explanation: The article argues that for AI to succeed in complex, dynamic, and policy-bound enterprise workflows, it needs structured guidance. Agent logic—software primitives like knowledge graphs and program analysis—steers the LLM, reducing context and improving performance.
mainPoints.point: Scalable enterprise AI requires 'agent logic', not just larger LLMs.

mainPoints.explanation: By pre-indexing information and guiding the LLM's focus, agent logic minimizes unnecessary context. The article cites examples like a 30x reduction in token consumption for legacy code understanding and up to 15x for test generation, directly impacting operational costs.
mainPoints.point: Agent logic dramatically reduces token consumption and cost.

mainPoints.explanation: Across multiple benchmarks (ITBench, AssetOpsBench), agents equipped with agent logic consistently outperformed baseline LLMs and even state-of-the-art coding agents. This includes up to 4.0x improvement in incident investigation and boosting compliance success rates from single digits to over 80%.
mainPoints.point: Agent logic improves performance and reliability over LLM-only approaches.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that scalable enterprise AI adoption depends not on larger LLMs but on integrating 'agent logic'—software primitives like knowledge graphs and program analysis—to guide models within complex workflows, achieving superior performance and cost-efficiency.
dataList.originalTitle: Beyond LLMs: Why Scalable Enterprise AI Adoption Depends on Agent Logic
dataList.summary: This article from IBM Research posits that the key to scalable enterprise AI adoption lies not in ever-larger language models, but in the strategic application of 'agent logic'. The authors define agent logic as software primitives—such as knowledge graphs, program analysis libraries, and algorithmic orchestration—that operate at the agentic layer to intentionally steer an LLM, reducing its context space and guiding it through complex, dynamic, and policy-constrained enterprise workflows. The article presents four detailed case studies from IBM's own products: 1) Legacy code modernization with watsonx Code Assistant for Z, achieving ~30x lower token consumption; 2) Automated test generation with Aster, showing 20-45% coverage improvements with up to 15x fewer tokens; 3) Proactive incident response with the Instana I3 agent, outperforming ReAct agents by up to 4.0x; and 4) IT compliance automation, boosting success rates from single digits to over 80%. Two additional domain case studies in healthcare and industrial maintenance further validate the approach. The core thesis is that agent logic provides the necessary 'GPS' for LLMs, enabling them to navigate enterprise systems with higher accuracy, lower cost, and greater reliability, thereby making scalable AI adoption a practical reality.

dataList.summary: This article profiles Jared Sires, an account executive at Anthropic who, despite having no prior coding experience, used Claude Code to build CLAFTS, an application that drafts customer email replies. The tool, built on roughly 4,300 lines of code written by Claude, integrates with Gmail, Google Drive, and web search to pull current product documentation and match Jared's writing style, saving him 10-15 hours per week. The success of CLAFTS led to a role shift: Jared is now a GTM product manager, building a suite of Claude-powered tools for the entire sales organization. These tools, packaged as a plugin for Claude Cowork, include daily briefs, customer context retrieval, pipeline management, and automated follow-up emails. The article details his iterative development process, the impact on his team (80% adoption within months), and his broader vision for using AI to dissolve technical barriers and empower non-engineers to build solutions.
